newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN torture body asks Israel to explain ruling.
newsitem.headline: UN torture body asks Israel to explain ruling.

text.p: The United Nations Committee against Torture on Friday asked the Israeli government to urgently explain a recent ruling by Israel's High Court which appears to sanction police use of physical force on detainees.
The letter, obtained by Reuters, said the court decision seemed to be "incompatible" with the Convention against Torture.
It reminded the Jewish state, which signed the pact in 1991, that "no exceptional circumstances whatsoever" -- neither war nor internal political instability -- justified torture.

On November 14, Israel's High Court overturned an interim court order which had forbidden Israel's Shin Bet secret police to use "physical force" against Palestinian detainees Muhammad Hamdan and Khedr Mubarak while interrogating them.
Both men are suspected of belonging to radical Islamist groups Jihad and Hamas, which were behind bomb attacks against the Jewish state which have killed scores of people.

"The Committee against Torture was informed by press agencies on 15 November 1996 that the Supreme Court of Israel has declared lawful the use of physical pressure by the Israeli security services in interrogating specific suspects of terrorist acts with a view to obtaining from them information which would prevent the perpetration of criminal acts in the future," the one-page letter read.

"The Committee takes the view that, if the information provided by press agencies is correct, the decision taken by the Supreme Court of Israel is incompatible with the provisions of the Convention," it added.
Composed of 10 independent experts, the body oversees compliance with the 1972 treaty, a major international human rights instrument ratified by 100 states.
The experts wound up their semi-annual, two-week meeting in Geneva on Friday, examining reports filed by six other states.
The letter from Committee chairman Alexis Dipanda Mouelle was addressed to Israel's ambassador in Geneva, Yosef Lamdan, for transmission to the government.

It requests that Israel report back to the Committee by January 31 so the experts can consider the matter at their next session starting on April 28. Israeli officials would be invited to participate in the discussion, according to the letter.

The letter said article two of the Convention "provides that no exceptional circumstances whatsoever, whether a state of war or a threat of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked as a justification of torture".

"Accordingly, the Committee invites the Government of Israel to submit as a matter of urgency a special report on the question of the decision taken by the Supreme Court and its implication for the implementation of the Convention in Israel."
Israel ratified the pact in 1991, but made certain "reservations", saying it could not accept articles which could allow the body to make a special inquiry.
Peter Burns, a Canadian legal expert on the Committee and its investigator for Israel, told a news briefing: "We can sympathise with the situation Israel confronts, everybody I think must.
But it is clear that the ends never justify the means."
"Very simply, when a state ratifies any international agreement it is bound by the terms of the agreement whatever its domestic situation might be," Burns added.
Israel had been due to file a regular report to the committee on its compliance with the Convention by November 1, but none has been received so far, officials said.
The report normally would be discussed at the April session.

A 1987 Israeli commission ruled the Shin Bet could use "moderate physical pressure" in interrogations and "increased physical pressure" when an attack was imminent. Human rights groups say that sanctioned torture.

Shin Bet officials have admitted in court cases to using methods such as violent shaking, which had already led to one death, prolonged sleep deprivation, and forcing detainees to remain in uncomfortable positions for long periods of time.
